text: In nineteen forty three, the United States Army set fire to its own air base. With bats.
It started with a dentist. Lytle Adams had just visited Carlsbad Caverns, home to hundreds of thousands of bats.
His idea: strap a tiny firebomb to every bat, drop them over Japanese cities, and let them hide under the roofs.
He wrote to the White House. President Roosevelt passed it on with a note: This man is not a nut.
So the military said yes. The inventor of napalm designed bombs small enough for a bat to carry.
To keep the bats calm, they were cooled in fridges until they fell asleep.
Then, during a test in May nineteen forty three, a few armed bats escaped.
They flew straight under a fuel tank. And the test base went up in flames.
Luckily, the bat bombs worked perfectly. Unluckily, they worked on America.
Why would it work? A normal bomb lands wherever it falls. A bat flies to the one place you would never check: the dark corner under your roof.
The Navy took over, spent about two million dollars, and then cancelled the whole thing in nineteen forty four.
The bat bombs never reached Japan. Their only victory was over the United States.
